book: 105 - The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die
essays: 1. Arya Stark as a Rough Hero
2. Ned Stark One Man in Ten Thousand
3. There’s Only One God and His Name Is Death
7. Jon Snow, a Misshapen Christ Figure
8. Brienne and the Struggle for Recognition
9. Varys’s Riddle—Where Does Power Come From
11. The Iron Bank Will Have Its Due
13. Bran, Hodor, and Disability in Westeros
16. Hope for Bastards and Sand Snakes
17. Sex, Consent, and Rape in Westeros
19. Prophetic Foreknowledge in Game of Thrones
samples: A short introduction that opens with the 'Hardhome' scene where Stannis tells Sam Tarly to 'keep reading' after learning from an old manuscript that dragonglass kills White Walkers, arguing that knowledge is itself a weapon in Westeros. Chaillan promises that the volume's philosophers ('Maester Kant on the King's Road,' 'Lord Machiavelli' in the Red Keep, Kierkegaard on Stannis) will initiate fans into the show's philosophical depth, from whether it is immoral to watch its violence to whether the Red Wedding can be justified.

Dadlez asks whether Game of Thrones is morally defective for making audiences root for Arya Stark, a child murderer whose victims run from the insurance seller in Braavos to Walder Frey and his sons baked into a pie. Working through Hume's 'rough heroes' worry from 'Of the Standard of Taste' against Anne Eaton's 'robust immoralism' and the halo effect, she argues Martin's text never endorses Arya's killings but shows their cost to her - her suppression of doubt before the soup-shop assassination, her nightmare repetition of the names on her kill list, her reclaiming of 'Arya Stark of Winterfell' - so our investment is empathetic concern rather than corrupting approval, and the story is not ethically flawed.

Kirby reads Ned Stark's arc through Aristotle's Poetics: his excessive honor is a hamartia ('too much of a good thing'), his acceptance of Robert's summons and refusal of Renly's help and Littlefinger's plan are the peripeteia, and the fan mourning after 'Baelor' is catharsis binding viewers into a community. With Martha Nussbaum's work on Greek tragedy he then argues the series' deepest lesson is tragic conflict - Agamemnon sacrificing Iphigenia mirrored by Stannis and Shireen, and Maester Aemon's 'love is the death of duty' warning to Jon - where no hierarchy of values dissolves the moral residue, so we must suffer into learning instead of trusting philosophical prioritization.

McKeever observes that central characters rarely die suddenly and unexpectedly in art even though such deaths define our emotional lives, and argues this is a 'representational limit of art,' like Hollywood ugliness and costume-drama archaic speech. Using Plato's theory of art as a copy of a copy (a picture of Tyrion's chipped goblet imitating the Form of the goblet) and Aristotle's catharsis, he then argues Martin overcomes the limit through epic scale: with so many viewpoint characters, Ned can die at the end of season one and Joffrey mid-season-four because attention simply shifts, so making a work epic is the general cure for what art cannot represent.

Hietalahti reads Tyrion's wit - slapping Joffrey, his mock confession at the Eyrie, the dwarf-jester show at the Purple Wedding - through the classic theories of humor: Kant and Kierkegaard's incongruity, the Platonic-Hobbesian superiority laugh, and Freud's hidden hostility. Against those who see only a jester, he argues Tyrion's humor is social criticism grounded in what Erich Fromm calls affirmation of life: unlike the Joker, who laughs because nothing matters, Tyrion mocks hollow ritual, sham trials, and gods who want enemies burned because everyone matters, and having lost everything in A Dance with Dragons he still refuses the poisonous 'sweet death,' holding that life itself is worth living.

Engels runs Tyrion's arc through Sartre's existentialism: his facticity as a dwarf makes everyone from Catelyn to Tywin presume his guilt, while 'Never forget what you are, wear it like armor' states the Sartrean authenticity of owning facticity while freely choosing one's essence. Catelyn's dagger accusation, the comic confession at the Eyrie, the wildfire ship at Blackwater, and the trial outburst ('I am guilty of a far more monstrous crime: the crime of being a dwarf') show him choosing rather than being defined; the murders of Shae and Tywin dramatize the slide into bad faith - embracing the 'monster' essence others assigned - before his choice to join Daenerys resumes the burden of self-creation.

book: 106 - Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!
essays: It Was a Dark and Philosophical Night
1. Charlie’s Eternal Quest for the Little Red-Haired Girl
4. Is it God or the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown
5. Rhapsody on a Theme by Schroeder
7. Life, Liberty and the Pursuit of a Warm Blanket
10. Does Snoopy Dream of Electric Sheep
12. Aaugh! Why Is Being Moral So Hard
14. Is Lucy a Kantian or Just Mean and Nasty
15. We’re on Your Side, Charlie Brown
samples: The editors' playful introduction stages the Peanuts gang together with Socrates, Plato, Descartes, Hume, Nietzsche, Wittgenstein, and Sartre at a Paris sidewalk cafe on the eve of Snoopy's dogfight with the Red Baron. It previews the seventeen essays' territory - the meaning of Christmas, kite-eating trees, the Great Pumpkin, baseball, critical thinking, induction, existence, happiness, virtue, friendship, ethics, and aesthetics - with the wink that to the kids it all sounds like 'Mwaa mwaa mwaa.'

The chapter reads Charlie Brown's lifelong, unconsummated longing for the never-seen Little Red-Haired Girl as a quest narrative without closure: like Beckett's Vladimir and Estragon he cannot act, and like Camus's Sisyphus he is an absurd hero whose dignity lies in persisting (the 2,120 lunch hours, the losing team, the pulled football) without reward. Using Lacan's account of desire - the wish for the Other's recognition, suspended between the demand for need and the demand for love - it argues Schulz keeps her invisible (except one 1998 silhouette) precisely so Charlie's desire stays in permanent suspension, like a Hitchcock MacGuffin. The closing section attacks The Peanuts Movie (2015) for betraying this existential vision: by showing the girl, rewarding Charlie with a kiss, and swapping Sisyphean defiance for 'believe in yourself' truisms, it delivers Sisyphus from his rock and so kills what made him admirable.

The chapter introduces existentialism and reads Peanuts through it: Charlie Brown's defeats expose the 'groundlessness' of value, and the 3eanuts web project (deleting each strip's final gag panel) restores the despair that punchlines normally defuse. It explains Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' and the ideal of authenticity versus passively inhabiting roles, Heidegger's care and Dasein (even in despair there is an inner place where it happens), and Camus's absurd and Sisyphus revolting against a fate he cannot change. Lucy's hillside sermon ('WELL, LIVE IN IT, THEN!') and the final image of Charlie running at the football figure his revolt: he keeps kicking because in that moment a world without boxes exists in him.

The chapter asks why Charlie Brown is unhappy despite being kind, active, and engaged, and answers with ancient virtue ethics: happiness is not winning or approval but ethical self-transformation, so his dependence on others' regard ('How did the other team feel?') is the real problem. It diagnoses him with Daniel Haybron's three dimensions of happiness - strong on engagement but lacking attunement (nervous, self-conscious) and endorsement (cheerlessness) - and asks why his shyness so irritates the gang. Epictetus's image of Socrates playing ball at his trial and Cicero's dancing analogy supply the Stoic remedy: losing costs no virtue, what he controls is being ethical, and how you play the game is everything.

Using It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown (1966), the chapter asks whether belief without evidence can be rational, contrasting the classic evidentialist view (rational beliefs must be basic or derived from basics, in the tradition of Locke and Hume) with Alvin Plantinga's properly basic beliefs and a virtue theory of rational belief built on Aristotle-style intellectual virtues like humility, courage, and charity. Linus fails on every account - he insulates himself from counterevidence ('If you really are a fake, don't tell me'), lets the belief cost him friends and trick-or-treating, and never updates after the Pumpkin's no-show - while Sally's pumpkin-patch vigil shows rationality as a balance of evidence, value, and risk. The upshot: God-belief formed responsibly within a trusting community can be rational in a way Linus's solitary, evidence-dodging Pumpkin faith cannot.

The chapter argues Schroeder's monomaniacal devotion to his toy piano and Beethoven is a Nietzschean way of life: he refuses the herd's path and the self-denying 'priestly' values of ordinary childhood, and treats music as the highest creative force, as The Birth of Tragedy claims. Nietzsche's demon of eternal recurrence becomes a test Schroeder passes - he lives for this life and could will its exact repetition - while Schopenhauer backs the claim that music discloses the world's inner nature as language cannot, and the Christmas-dance scene shows the communal fusion Nietzsche heard in song and dance. Strips about Lucy on the piano, his 'grown accustomed to that face' shock when she moves away, and the Beethoven's-birthday holiday cast Lucy as his unsuspecting muse; but as a would-be Ubermensch he must go beyond playing Beethoven and create his own compositions.

book: 107 - Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling
essays: 3. The Only Chapter in This Book You Need to Read!
4. How Much Deadpool Is Too Much Deadpool
8. How Shitty Can a Hero Be
10. Always a Pallbearer, Never the Corpse
16. The Beautiful Face Behind the Mask
17. Wade Wilson Fights Like a Girl
samples: Editor Nicolas Michaud's introduction argues Deadpool brings an 'obscene number of philosophical questions'—about mortality, morality, the multiverse, killing, and what separates hero, villain, and asshole—and that only waiting for a movie delayed this book. It proposes that philosophers should be more like Deadpool: honest enough to admit no one knows the answers, willing to look into the abyss, laugh, and jump in anyway, and ready to tell unwelcome truths even if it makes them villains. The tone-setting piece closes with bawdy fourth-wall-style gags about the book being 'better than sex' and unlicensed by Deadpool.

Rhiannon Grant argues Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks make him a great philosopher and sociologist because they enact the examined life: like Socrates's unexamined-life dictum, Deadpool steps outside his world to ask new questions about it ('Stewart or McAvoy?'), and even examines his own habit of examining—the 'sixteen walls' break inside a break. Wittgenstein's fly-bottle becomes the trap of circular philosophical argument that Deadpool escapes by seeing the bottle from outside, while Berkeley's solipsism is the failed attempt to live as if the world existed only in one's mind. A closing dialogue has Professor X coach Deadpool through insider/outsider research ethics and objectivity (the sperm-and-egg microscope example), showing how fourth-wall skill lets a researcher view a community from both inside and outside.

Christopher Ketcham playfully argues that Deadpool's fourth-wall escapes show he exists partly in dimensions we cannot experience, read through string theory's ten curled dimensions and Maimonides's ten realms of angels—beings of form without matter—in the Mishneh Torah. Since only God and angels traverse those hidden dimensions, Deadpool must be an angel, likely a dark one, whose shuttling between realms explains his vacillation between mercenary violence and saving souls. Ezekiel's chariot vision, the vengeful Hebrew Bible God, and massless dark matter are recruited as supporting evidence for this deadpan-earnest science-and-scripture argument.

Writing as two bickering versions of himself from different universes, Karavitis reads Deadpool Kills Deadpool as showing that the multiverse of Deadpools is the delusion of a single narcissist: the alternate 'Pools' are mirror-image projections of himself (Lacan's mirror stage), his self-love is Rousseau's pathological amour propre rather than healthy amour de soi, and his claim to be the progenitor of all reality is solipsism—hence there is no fourth wall. Freud, Fromm, and Marcuse supply rival diagnoses of that narcissism, from arrested development to proto-fascist willfulness to authentic rebellion against social control through unconscious conformity. A closing twist argues philosophers who claim sole access to truth are the same solipsistic narcissists, which would make Socrates, who never claimed a final answer, the only true philosopher.

The chapter argues Deadpool is entertaining because of, not despite, his excesses: his gratuitous violence and rapid-fire wisecracks breach the disciplined hero ideal, measured against Zeno of Citium's stoic dichotomy of control (accept the torture you cannot change, master your response) and Aristotle's golden mean between deficient and excessive force, which Wade flouts when he savors punishing Ajax instead of finishing quickly. Bakhtin's carnival excess explains the grotesque, orifice-obsessed humor that mocks 'normal' decency, and Derrida's 'internal drifting' (via Poe's Purloined Letter) frames Deadpool's first appearance being FedExed back to sender and his threshold position, where gags spill across comic, game, and film frames—making vigilante justice 'a supplement to the supplement' of law and exposing how each medium works.

Andy Vink applies Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, in the Power of Myth version where heroism is a transformation of consciousness from selfishness to self-sacrifice, to the Duggan-Posehn arc 'The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly'. Deadpool starts self-centered—demanding pillowcases of money for killing zombie Presidents—is transformed by revelations (Dr. Butler holding his daughter Eleanor hostage, the North Korean mutate experiments echoing his own Weapon X trauma), and ends risking himself to free Butler's sister and the captive mutates and their families. The verdict: Deadpool genuinely becomes a hero by Campbell's test, which is also why, in Campbell's scheme, the hero never gets the girl.

book: 109 - Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp
essays: 2. If I Don’t Listen to My Imaginary Friend, Why the Fuck Should I Listen to Yours
7. What Kind of Revolutionary Is Mr. Robot
8. Mr. Robot, Mad Son of Noir
9. What Elliot Doesn’t Know Won’t Hurt You (Or Will It )
10. If It Isn’t Justified Is It Still My Revolution
11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them
14. Is E Corp an Evil Person
19. Please Tell Me You’re Seeing This Too
samples: The volume's introduction is written in Elliot's paranoid voice, doubting whether the book, the reader, or reality itself exist. It lays out the questions the essays will tackle: fsociety's hack of the Evil Corporation, whether it was political ideology or revenge for the corporation killing Elliot's and Darlene's father, whether either motive (or hacking in general) can be justified, and what order could survive after the financial system falls.

Rocha reads fsociety's 5/9 logic-bomb attack on E Corp as anarchist 'propaganda of the deed' - a shocking act meant to wake people from their comfortable slumber inside hierarchy - and positions it between Alexander Berkman's violent anarchism (mirroring Phillip Price's 'bullet in the right place') and Gandhi's nonviolent self-suffering, quoting satyagraha and the older Goldman's rejection of violence. He then runs the hack through just war theory's four questions (necessity, proportionality, justification, effectiveness), noting that wiping the debt records also destroyed savings and indirectly got people like Gideon killed, and that fsociety, as Trenton says, never paints the alternative society - so the reader is left to answer whether the deed was justified.

Kreider stages a chat between Plato and Aristotle about the show. On Plato's account, mimesis is an imitation of an imitation of the Forms, so Elliot's imaginary friend, his fake persona with Krista, and the Mr. Robot personality are intellectually and morally dangerous deceptions that let him commit terrorism without his rational self's consent; yet the Republic's censored poetry for the auxiliaries explains how fsociety's masked videos teach true beliefs, and how Elliot uses the fictional Mr. Robot to educate himself toward ideas he already knew were right. Aristotle's Poetics then defends imitation as natural and instructive - the show is a cautionary tragedy, and the Mr. Robot crutch is how Elliot eventually steps up to claim responsibility.

Porot reads Elliot through Berlin's positive liberty: people are enslaved to their lower selves - the 'daemons' of addiction and primal urge Elliot describes in 'eps1.3_da3m0ns.mp4' - and freedom requires a contract in which an external force holds you to your higher self. Elliot writes such contracts with Shayla over his drugs and imagines Mr. Robot as the paternalistic enforcer who pushes him off the pier when he breaks his word, while corporations run the reverse contract, 'hacking' people from within through addictive sugar, clickbait, and advertising. The black fish dream crystallizes this: everyone at the office devours the confined fish of reverse-contract slavery while Elliot alone eats Pop's pie - freedom through the father figure of Mr. Robot.

Brake reads Mr. Robot through Thomas More's Utopia: Hythloday's 'conspiracy of the rich' matches E Corp's Washington Township cover-up, his attacks on private property echo Elliot's monologue about property and money, and the island with 'nothing private anywhere' frames the provocative idea that the veil of privacy shelters corporate injustice that only lawbreaking - fsociety's hacks, Manning, Snowden, Assange - can lift into daylight. Yet More splits himself between idealist Hythloday and pragmatic More, and the messy aftermath of the 5/9 hack shows that utopian dreams implemented without caution can become nightmares.

Ketcham updates Hobbes for the network age: the grid born of ARPANET and Cold War mutual destruction has devolved into a new state of nature, out of which a coming 'Leviathan' - the one percent of the one percent - will rule invisibly by curating your memories, your purchases, your spouse, and whole countries like the diamond-republic fable. Invoking Descartes's evil demon and Heidegger's ready-to-hand, he asks whether we have become the grid, an external brain we can no longer control, and concludes that Elliot, the rogue 'Ebola' who hacks for justice rather than profit, is exactly the loose cannon Leviathan would quarantine.

book: 111 - The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality
essays: 4. Cruel Optimism and the Good Nazi Life
5. In the Neutral Zone, a Libertarian’s Home Is Their (High) Castle
7. What if Your Hero Is a Fascist
8. Is It Free Will If You Pay for It
9. Could the Axis Have Won the War
12. Are We Really Sure They’re Wrong
13. But Why Is Our World Better
16. How Close Is That World to Our World
18. How to Deal with Reality when We’re not Built To
samples: Dennis Weiss argues the Amazon series is really about television and screened images: Juliana screening the Grasshopper newsreel in her basement replays Plato's Cave, except that the projected images, not the 'real' world of Nazi America, are what offer her 'a way out.' Following her from transfixed belief to doubt (calling the final film 'a nightmare' and choosing to trust Joe over the reel), and reading the show's media surfaces (Nazi commercials, 'Edelweiss,' the Riefenstahl comparison, Tagomi's cross-world vision), the chapter uses media thinkers like McLuhan, Meyrowitz, and Don Ihde to describe learning to see with 'compound vision' in a placeless, image-saturated culture.

Reading the show's Nazi-remade monuments (the swastika on Mount Rushmore and the Statue of Liberty, the SS tower, VA Day spectacle) through Walter Benjamin's account of fascism as aestheticized politics that narcotizes the masses, the chapter argues architecture is what makes the alternate timeline legible to viewers. It then contrasts these fixed 'words in stone' with 'counter-monuments' that keep alternative memory alive: the clandestinely circulating newsreels, Frank and Mark's underground Hebrew prayer, and the fragile chrysanthemums Tagomi and Juliana exchange, with Tagomi's final vision of a Lolita-billboard San Francisco recognized through buildings alone.

The chapter claims the show takes dualism — the same physical world with different 'histories' as its mind — and multiplies it into many overlapping versions of each person: Juliana and Frank swap awe and fear between the first and ninth episodes' screenings, and the newsreel in which Joe executes Frank shifts how they see the real Joe. Its centerpiece is the finale, where viewers find themselves rooting for the Nazis Smith and Wegener to keep Hitler alive and prevent a worse war, forcing the audience to confront its own shifting allegiances and how easily fascism could take root in America.

Applying Lauren Berlant's 'cruel optimism,' the chapter argues John Smith and Frank Frink are ruined by the very 'good life' they pursue under the Reich: Smith sustains the system of suburban family, VA Day rituals, and housewife-training daughters until Thomas's Dejerine-Roussy diagnosis makes the eugenic order threaten his own son, while Frank clings to settling down with Juliana and keeps choosing escape over resistance even after his sister's murder. Bertrand Russell's definition of the good life as 'inspired by love and guided by knowledge,' together with Henri Lefebvre's need/desire contrast and Jonathan Crary on television's anti-nomadic passivity, supplies the measuring stick this world fails to meet.

The chapter reads Dick as a left-leaning libertarian for whom the deepest evil of the High Castle world is the loss of privacy: Arnold's surveillance unit and the Kempeitai's wiretaps illustrate Locke's self-ownership and natural rights, while the Neutral Zone poses the Hobbesian question of whether even an oppressive state beats the state of nature, and the 'libertarian minimal state' names what the Reich destroys. On this reading the American Nazis like John Smith were internal collaborators all along — 'it already happened here' — and ethics lies in refusal, as when Tagomi declines to sign the order sending Frank to his death.

Marc Cole argues the Reich's and Japan's governments have the structure of Plato's Republic: supreme power in a political expert who is above the law and manages citizens' work, breeding, education, and music from cradle to grave — in some ways more controlling than the Nazis, since Plato abolishes the family outright. John Smith's son Thomas, condemned to death by a law blind to particular circumstances, embodies the Statesman's 'self-willed and ignorant' law, and after weighing the doctor/patient defense of rule by expertise, the chapter sides with democratic republics and warns that multiplying laws and state management inches us toward Plato's republic or the Reich.

book: 112 - The Americans and Philosophy - Reds in the Bed
essays: 3 On the Origin of the Family
4 On the Origin of the State
5 The Changing Bases of Sexual Politics, 1960–2020
6 Wives and Husbands The Marital Power Struggle
samples: Smith introduces his project of explaining the subordination of women and blacks philosophically and empirically by comparing the social contract liberalism of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau with Marxism, building on Carole Pateman's Sexual Contract and Charles Mills's Racial Contract/Contract and Domination, which show the classic contracts were male supremacist and white supremacist. He argues sexual and racial egalitarianism is about politics and power, cataloguing nine power bases women and blacks should acquire, and stresses that because family and state are historically connected (Aristotle's Politics, Hobbes's 'little kingdoms', Locke's conjugal society, Rousseau's family as the oldest society, Engels's 'first class oppression' of the female by the male), equality in marriage may be a precondition for equality in society. He defends Marxism against Mills's dismissal of it as moribund, endorses MacKinnon's linking of sexism and racism while arguing (with Linda LaRue and Du Bois) that the racial contract has been more tyrannical than the sexual contract, and closes with Walzer's definition of egalitarianism as a society free of domination.

The chapter traces politics from the classical ethics-fused view (Aristotle's Politics, where politics exists for the sake of the good life yet also supplies one of the first justifications of patriarchy and the public/private split) to the Machiavelli-Hobbes break where politics becomes simply the possession and exercise of power, adopting Bertrand Russell's claim that power is the fundamental concept of social science. It then builds the book's central instrument, a Weber-derived analysis of nine power bases (money, knowledge/technology/information, religion, morality, authority, charisma, size/solidarity, violence, status), contrasting the Marxian reading - money as ultimately determinative, the ruling ideas of each age as the ideas of the ruling class, religion as the opium of the people, the state as a committee for managing bourgeois affairs - with the liberal-Weberian reading in which no single base is decisive. It closes by showing that Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau and Marx divide over the morality of egalitarianism (Popper's Marx moved by moral impulse versus Locke's possessive individualism), and that power is domain-specific, inert until used, skill-dependent and always relative.

The chapter compares the liberal contract theorists with Engels (building on Morgan's Ancient Society) on the origin of the patriarchal monogamous family: Hobbes derives sovereign-husbanded 'little monarchies' from a state of nature in which women are men's equals, a derivation Susan Okin shows is contradictory; Locke grounds conjugal society in a voluntary compact with the husband as 'abler and stronger' last determiner, yet leaves women excluded from the social contract; Rousseau pairs passionate economic equality with some of the most sexist writing in Western thought, including fear of wives' sexual power in Emile. Against these static philosophies Engels gives a historical-materialist account in which the overthrow of mother right - the 'world historical defeat of the female sex' - followed from private property and inheritance, turning the bourgeois wife into a proletarian or prostitute while opening 'sex love' to the propertyless, and prescribing women's return to the labor force, socialized child-care, industrialized housework and easy divorce. John Stuart Mill's Subjection of Women appears as liberalism's one exception to its sexism, and a footnote sets Firestone's biological account of patriarchy against Engels's property account.

Opening with Newt Gingrich's complaint that students 'don't read enough Locke' and the Chinese premier's appeal to Rousseau, the chapter compares the three contract theorists' states of nature and purposes of government: Hobbes's war of every man against every man yielding an absolute sovereign with no separation of powers, Locke's peaceful nature in which mixing labor with land creates property and money then creates inequality, so that government's 'great and chief end' is protecting property through limited, separated powers and no food stamps, and Rousseau's compassionate natural humans corrupted when the first man enclosed land, so the state was founded on fraud and a general will that should 'force him to be free' and give people food stamps. Smith then reads the actual US founding as a chaste Lockean contract 'bastardized' on race and sex - the Declaration plagiarized from Locke, Abigail Adams's 'remember the ladies' laughed off, Dred Scott, with the 14th Amendment as the de-bastardizing 'Charter of Universal Freedom' - while Engels derives the state historically from the Iroquois and Greek gens, private property and class conflict. A final section documents white supremacy inside the tradition (Kant inventing the scientific concept of race, Hegel and Hume on Black inferiority), John Stuart Mill's 'Negro Question' as the tradition's decisive anti-racist break, Locke's own entanglements with the slave trade, and Marx's condemnation of slavery as super-exploitation.

Measuring women's progress since 1960 by access to the nine power bases, the chapter shows women using the size/solidarity base to launch the modern feminist movement - Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique as its manifesto, NOW as its vehicle, Ms. as its outlet and Gloria Steinem as its charismatic leader - and how law followed: the accidental Smith amendment adding sex to the 1964 Civil Rights Act, Reed and Frontiero subjecting sex classifications to scrutiny under the 14th Amendment, Griswold and Roe/Casey making reproductive control (which Justice Blackmun called 'necessary for the complete emancipation of women') a condition of women's power, and the 1970s no-fault divorce revolution that Engels's liberation program had demanded. It then charts each base statistically: the narrowing labor-force and wage gaps, women's still minor share of the bourgeoisie, the reversal of the college gender gap and Women's Studies programs built on the Black Studies model, women's entry into cabinet, Court, Congress, clergy and the military, secularization that weakens the religion base behind Elizabeth Cady Stanton's old challenge, and a new moral consensus that unequal treatment of women is wrong.

Taking Susan Okin's 'the personal is political' and Kate Millett's Weberian herrschaft against Locke's public/private dichotomy, the chapter reviews the empirical studies of marital power (Blood and Wolfe, Blumstein and Schwarz, Steil) and finds money is the master base in marriage: the husband's income and occupational prestige set his say, working wives gain power but couples conspire to understate wives' earnings ('manning up and womaning down'), while knowledge and status are the next strongest resources. Authority from religion, tradition and morality still favors husbands (Ephesians' 'wives submit yourselves unto your husbands' alongside the philosophers' 'abler and stronger'), violence persists from the rule of thumb to marital rape and murder despite legal change, housework remains women's burden - Beauvoir's never-won 'battle against dust', Engels's 'leaden boredom', Davis's industrialization proposal and Okin's demand that it be shared - and sex itself works as a power base in the bedroom, with MacKinnon diagnosing heterosexuality as the linchpin of gender inequality. The chapter ends with black couples' comparatively egalitarian patterns traced by Angela Davis to slave-quarters equality, Schwarz's rare 'peer marriages', and the Marxist (Okin, the Swedish model) versus liberal (Wilson, the Japanese model) readings of family change.

book: 113 - Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required
essays: 1. I Stand Up Next to a Mountain
2. Zen and the Art of Guitar Burning
6. Quicker than the Wink of an Eye
12. The Broken Pieces of Yesterday’s Life
16. Artistic Expression in the Land of the Free
samples: Editorial introduction tracing the successive identities of Johnny Allen Hendrix, James Marshall Hendrix, Jimmy James, and Jimi — from Seattle and the chitlin' circuit with the Isley Brothers and Little Richard to Chas Chandler's London — arguing there was no single Hendrix but a series of continual transformations. It dismisses a 'Hegelian unfolding of The Absolute' that would require true blues musicians to be born in the South, and speculates that the Jimi lost in 1970 was a would-be jazz-blues synthesizer, reading 'Rainy Day, Dream Away' and 'Still Raining, Still Dreaming' as evidence and invoking the rumored Miles Davis collaboration.

Reads Hendrix as Joseph Campbell's hero on the monomyth of separation, initiation, and return: the mother's death and gypsy prophecy of 'Voodoo Chile' stage the separation, the Venus witch's ring the initiation, and the transcending guitar solo the return, with Prometheus as the type of the fire-bringer punished by promoters, Little Richard, and audiences demanding the hits. Through Nietzsche's Birth of Tragedy it casts the Monterey guitar-burning and the Dionysian intensity of the Experience as tragic art whose hero 'shoulders the whole Dionysiac world for us,' and closes with Aristotle's Politics on catharsis — 'Machine Gun''s sonic battle imagery as purgation that transforms violence into a cry for peace.

Argues Hendrix's art worked like a Zen transmission outside words and doctrine: Nansen's cat, the Buddha's silent flower sermon, Zeami's hidden flower in Noh, and Linji burning the sutras frame the guitar-burning, playing with his teeth, and the backwards tape of 'Are You Experienced?' as skillful means that shock listeners out of dualistic discrimination into pure suchness. The Woodstock sequence — the 'Star-Spangled Banner' followed seamlessly by 'Purple Haze' and the 'Instrumental Solo' — is read as an eschatological passage from the death-symbolism of the national anthem to a Zen-like experiential beginning, with Hendrix acting as a Bodhisattva whose Stratocaster is the master's stick of compassion.

Contends that Hendrix's discord is philosophy-as-discord: 'I Don't Live Today' (the Native American dead-in-life), the Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' with its bombs and sirens against sporting-event sentimentality, 'Machine Gun,' and 'House Burning Down' lacerate listeners so they actually feel war's atrocities instead of parroting patriotic clichés. Against this the chapter sets the oceanic, womb-like escape fantasies of '1983 (A Merman I Should Turn to Be)' and 'Valleys of Neptune,' treating them through Schopenhauer as metaphysical consolation, Marx's opiate, and Nietzsche's 'hangman's metaphysics,' and concludes that Hendrix finally refuses such world-denying illusions — and Heideggerian inauthentic withdrawal — in favor of existential engagement with suffering here and now.

The editor asks where Hendrix's 'bestness' lies by testing whether he was ever free: his songs demand freedom ('If 6 Was 9,' 'Stone Free,' 'Freedom,' 'Ezy Ryder') but never assert that the human condition is free, and his caffeine-style appetites, exploitative contracts, and management suggest determination rather than liberty. A detour through 'Hey Joe' as premeditated murder — compared with Othello and the Ice-T 'Cop Killer' affair — argues that fabricated narrators make it impossible to glean an artist's own moral sense from songs. He concludes that Hendrix's deepest mastery was the treatment of love, from 'The Wind Cries Mary' to 'Little Wing,' making him the sixties' most powerful spokesman for love rather than freedom, per the quoted 'when the power of love overcomes the love of power.'

Traces 'genius' from the indwelling genie of an art to Goethe as the first person the public called a genius, then applies Kant's doctrine — the genius gives the rule to future art, produces what no determinate rule can govern, and cannot explain or teach what he does — to Jimi (having the Experience learn 'Sgt. Pepper' on one hearing to play it back to the Beatles three days after its release), Janis ('a victim of my own insides'), and Jim. Schopenhauer's dark side of genius — more mind than character, a will that 'affirms its own life by denying the life of others' — explains why the 27 Club burned out, and why we say 'Jimi lives' but 'Jim is still alive.'

book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare
essays: The Devil Made Us Write This
1. What’s So Scary about Demonic Possession
4. How to Live through a Horror Story and Still Find Your Self
7. And the Most Despicable Jessica Lange Character Is . .
12. A Month from Now, I’ll Be a Balding, Toothless Skeleton
14. The Absurdity at the Heart of Horror
16. Please Don’t Kill Me! (But if You Do, Could You Make a Video )
samples: The editors' introduction argues that American Horror Story is 'American' in its maximalist excess (the pilot's creepy house, breathing disemboweled cat, and bloody murder), in recycling every major American horror trope from vampires, witches, and ghosts to freak shows and slasher clowns, and in its social commentary on marginalized groups, race relations, and civil rights - so that stripped of horror it is about life in America, and underneath the gore it contains 'a lot of great philosophy', which the book's sixteen chapters extract.

Using the Asylum possession arc - the boy who rips open the pig's heart, the demon exposing Sister Jude's hit-and-run secret and whispering 'You're Bloody Face' to Thredson, and Sister Mary Eunice's corruption - the chapter argues that possession stories terrify because they break our identity judgments through time, the same judgments on which moral responsibility, criminal punishment (the Manson family parole cases, Phineas Gage), trust, and personal safety depend. Descartes's mind-body union and psychological-continuity theories of identity explain why sameness of body can no longer guarantee sameness of person, and why we fear our own identity being erased next.

Argues that dying in the Murder House or the Hotel Cortez removes death's usual harms - Ben Harmon can reunite with his ghost family and keep counseling patients, and Liz Taylor's chosen death brings reunion with Tristan plus open-ended projects protecting the hotel - but then poses Bernard Williams's boredom problem: finite projects run out over eternity and replacing them would make you a different person. Richard Taylor's Sisyphus and the Hotel's contented Laundress supply the answer that repetitive tasks embraced as meaningful can sustain even an immortal afterlife.

Staged as a remembered backstage conversation among Elsa's freak show performers, the chapter has conjoined twins Bette and Dot work through the Ship of Theseus, the psychological-continuity theory of identity and its coma and false-memory counterexamples, Quine's claim that persons are only convenient posits rather than real entities, split-brain cases suggesting one body can host two minds, and fission worries about what would happen if they were separated - to ask whether they are one person or two, concluding it is a genuine paradox with no agreed answer.

A survival guide built on Charles Taylor's philosophy of the self: reality 'discloses' different possibilities depending on one's attunement (Ben Harmon sees the young Moira, the Harmons and the Roanoke families misread their houses), the medieval enchanted cosmos of porous selves explains Sister Mary Eunice's demon, the cursed rubber suit, and Billie Dean Howard's trauma-soaked houses, while the buffered self of the disenchanted universe - Arden locating the devil in the frontal gyrus, John Lowe demanding evidence - invites gaslighting, and full porousness brings its own horrors (Kyle, Cricket). The lesson: keep a pragmatic, open mind and share reality with a community.

Explains Kyle Spencer's horror at the body Madison and Zoe assembled from other people's parts through the history of soul-body theories: Aristotle's De Anima account of the soul as the faculties of a living body (plus the Physiognomonics claim that small people have small minds - poor Ma Petite), Plato's Timaeus on body parts designed for philosophy and reincarnation into bodies fitted to one's vices, Avicenna's soul as a faculty-binding nexus that chooses its bodily vehicle like a vehicle serves its owner, and Merleau-Ponty's habitual body (the Axeman's axe as part of his body, phantom limbs), which best explains why walking around on someone else's legs 'has got to mess with you a little'.

book: 115 - Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe
essays: 1. How to Fail at Almost Everything and Still Be a Hero
3. Will the Real American Hero Please Stand Up
4. He’s a Hero in a Bottle, Baby
5. Why the Good Man Is a Great Leader
7. How Captain America and Iron Man Embody America
8. Believing the Impossible in a World of Compromise
11. Fighting Ethical Relativism in Tales of Suspense
12. Champion of the People vs. Technology
16. Would You Buy a Used Car from This Avenger
17. Please Hold for a Call from God
18. Red vs. Blue or Both Simply Leviathan Green
19. The Superhero Challenge to State Sovereignty
samples: The editors' introduction frames the whole book around one question: not just which hero would win, but who is right, Iron Man or Captain America. It argues the matchup terrifies and fascinates because both are our good guys - Stark the test of whether we can love a ragingly selfish capitalist, Rogers the wartime-propaganda patriot who punched Hitler - and their Civil War clash stages every American's internal war between safety and freedom.

Malloy argues Iron Man is the better hero precisely because he fails constantly - Armor Wars, the Registration Act, alcoholism, a string of collapsed Stark companies - while Steve Rogers was born heroic and never stumbles. Using Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, he treats perseverance as a virtue between cowardly quitting and Cap's stubborn excess (his doomed stand against Thanos in Infinity Gauntlet), and separates Tony's virtuous perseverance from Dr. Doom's identical behavior by its motives: Tony honestly examines his failures to help people, while Doom only looks for someone to blame.

McCrossin builds a six-part definition of heroism (moral, altruistic, atypical, supererogatory, replicable safeguarding) and tests it on Wesley Autrey versus Captain Sullenberger and a Super Autrey thought experiment: Iron Man's engineering-based feats are refinements of abilities we share and so inspire imitation, while there can only ever be one Captain America, making Tony the more heroic. The Sokovia Accords debate then contrasts two humilities, with Stark's willingness to accept oversight more heroic than Rogers' safest-hands-are-our-own confidence. The chapter closes by explaining why we invent super heroes at all through Susan Neiman's account of the problem of evil after twentieth-century atrocities, from the Stamford explosion to Charlie Spencer's death in Lagos.

Samuelson argues Tony Stark is the real American hero because he embodies the Locke-to-Smith lineage of American values - natural rights, property from mixing labor, free trade and the invisible hand, plus Smithian sympathy - carried forward into twenty-first-century neoliberalism, from Stark Industries to backing the Registration Act. Steve, by contrast, keeps abandoning the Captain America identity (Nomad after the Secret Empire, The Captain under Nuke's government, handing the shield to Bucky and Sam Wilson) whenever America betrays the dream, and admits his true fight is against bullies and for human rights everywhere. Hence Cap is a great hero but not strictly an American one, while Tony lives American values practically, warts and all.

Insooks deploys Nietzsche to argue Iron Man is the better hero: Cap's prized humility and relatability are sheep morality, the resentful herd value that drags the excellent down to average (as when society savored the Olympic swimmer's fall), while Tony honestly owns his superiority and keeps self-overcoming, building ever-better suits rather than resting on a serum gifted in a bottle. On this view Cap's manufactured modesty insults people who genuinely struggle, and the true super hero inspires from the mountaintop - build yourself a suit and get up here - instead of pretending to be just like us.

Nisley reads Civil War through Aristotle's good man and good leader: Cap shows courage but lacks temperance and practical wisdom - his rash Lagos operation, his rage-borne beating of Tony, his choice of Bucky over the Avengers' common end - and his ceaseless struggle between passion and reason falls short of virtue. Applying Aristotle's account of philia, she argues the Avengers are a friendship of the virtuous that requires deliberation toward justice, which Cap dissolves by tearing the team apart, while Tony's reasoned acceptance of UN oversight, moderation after Ultron, and concern for the whole team make him the good man fit to lead.

essays: 3. Why Don’t the Proles Just Take Over
5. Ministry of Truth Handbook Excerpt on the Strategic Use of Fallacious Reasoning for Thoughtcrime Prevention
13. Hangings, Shootings, and Other Funny Stuff in 1984
samples: The editors answer Asimov's and Posner's dismissals of 1984 as obsolete by pointing to the Iraq War's 935 false statements, Snowden's NSA surveillance disclosures, weaponized social media, and Kellyanne Conway's 'alternative facts' as evidence that we may live in Orwell's world in 2018. They argue technology is not the antidote to Orwellian concerns, despite Apple's famous '1984 won't be like Nineteen Eighty-Four' ad, since telescreen-like smartphones and the Party's history-rewriting bureaucracy are both forms of 'political technology'. The real antidote is philosophy, which trains us to examine assumptions and resist bad arguments, as Winston feared when he thought any Party intellectual could overthrow him in debate.

Storrie and Martin use Foucault's critique of the repressive hypothesis to argue that Winston is wrong to think sex is naturally subversive and the Party merely represses it. Power over sexuality is productive: the Soviet sexual revolution, Ceausescu's Decree 770 and its 'Decree Generation', Pornosec's pornography for pacifying proles, and tacitly tolerated prostitution all channel erotic energy into state power rather than simply forbid it. Reading O'Brien's torture of Winston as a sustained scene of rape and castration (following Cass Sunstein), they conclude that only understanding power's productive use of sex, as Julia does, makes effective resistance possible; it is Winston who turns out to be merely 'a revolutionary from the waist down'.

Di Nucci compares the Party's mandatory morning Physical Jerks to the modern middle-class ritual of pre-work exercise, asking who needs an oppressor when we oppress ourselves. He argues exercise carries a hidden political price: the time, energy, and solitude it consumes (Orwell shows exercise making it harder for Winston to think and remember) leave citizens too exhausted for the political engagement Aristotle considered necessary to the good life. Like Juvenal's bread and circuses, now 'panem et iphones', and like private schooling, fitness culture also deepens class inequality because working-class people lack the time and energy to access it.

Littmann asks why Oceania's proles, 85 percent of the population who could 'blow the Party to pieces tomorrow morning', never revolt, answering with Winston's diagnosis: until they become conscious they will never rebel. The Party keeps them unconscious through its media monopoly, crimestop, doublethink, reality control, perpetual war hysteria, and a nationalist identity that cuts them off from the international proletariat. He maps each mechanism onto the modern US, where six corporations control about 90 percent of media, citizens tailor their own reality bubbles, opponents are assumed to argue in bad faith, and partisan 'nationalisms' block common cause, arguing that American political conflict is mostly over facts rather than values.

Nash argues 1984 has been misread as a critique of state power alone; through Newspeak's silencing of thought (in the tradition Austin, MacKinnon, and Langton developed) it shows how any concentration of power oppresses via control of words, data, and information. Drawing on Goldstein's manual's debt to James Burnham's managerial revolution and Sheldon Wolin's 'inverted totalitarianism', she reads the non-centralized Oceania as a warning about non-state enemies: corporations, think tanks running the 'Tobacco Strategy', and global institutions peddling misleading poverty statistics. Popper, Arendt, and Berlin exemplify the state-focused liberalism she thinks blinded us to these horizontal threats, while the Newspeak appendix's past tense shows Orwell expected totalitarianism to be beatable through evidence and democracy.

Rard's satirical Party handbook explains how to keep a population from thinking: keep the proles too poor and exhausted to reason, and deploy fallacies strategically, from ad hominem goat-caricatures of Goldstein at the Two Minutes Hate and straw man versions of his arguments, to destroying contrary evidence, appealing to fear of the old capitalist world, and Room 101's appeal to force, so false beliefs can be manufactured as easily as true ones. It presents Plato's noble lie as the Ministry's founding inspiration, calling the reader's mission 'a continuation of Plato's dream'. It also cites Aristotle's view that emotion must be disciplined for reason to work, which the Party inverts by deliberately triggering fear and hatred to disable rational thought.
